idiom_name: ConcurrentHashMap[String, Promise[Reply]] + firstCompletedOf with a scheduled timeout
implementation_notes: scala.concurrent.Promise is the completer paired with a Future, so the table is a ConcurrentHashMap of promises and the transport callback resolves the matching one with trySuccess/tryFailure; the deadline is a second future produced by a scheduler and combined with Future.firstCompletedOf (or Await.result with a duration for blocking callers). Promise is stdlib, so no dependency is needed, but the pattern is not absorbed into the language: the id, the table and the timeout policy are still yours, and an uncompleted promise retains its callbacks and the state they close over. Completing through trySuccess keeps the late-reply path exception-free.
pitfalls: Promise#success throws IllegalStateException when the promise is already completed; always use trySuccess/tryFailure so a duplicate or late reply is a no-op.
A promise that is never completed retains its callbacks and everything they capture - the timeout path must complete it (tryFailure), not merely remove it from the map.

scala.concurrent.Future cannot be cancelled: timing out the caller does not stop the request, so the id has to stay reserved (or the reply explicitly dropped) or the next request can match a stale reply.
The scheduled timeout future must come from an execution context that stays alive; a scheduler that shuts down silently turns every deadline into a caller that waits forever.

variants.name: Akka ask: temporary actor as the correlator
variants.idiom_name: ActorRef replyTo field / AskPattern.ask temporary actor
variants.implementation_notes: The actor model supplies the association structurally instead of with an id: the sender encodes its own ActorRef in the message (replyTo), or uses ask, which creates a temporary actor whose reference is the correlation handle, and the replier simply tells the response to that address - no shared table and no id space. The Akka documentation makes the trade-off explicit: unless the protocol already carries a request id, an interaction cannot be tied to a specific context, which is exactly why ask introduces the temporary actor. Choose this variant when the system is already actor-based; the promise map remains the right tool for a raw socket or queue transport that cannot address an actor.
pitfalls: ask needs an ActorSystem, an implicit Timeout and a scheduler: the future fails with AskTimeoutException and the temporary actor only keeps the reply address alive for that window.

A response sent to a stopped or wrong replyTo is dead-lettered silently, which is the actor world's unknown correlation id - watch the dead-letter stream instead of assuming a lost reply is a network fault.
One temporary actor per call is expensive in hot paths; for high fan-out prefer a protocol that carries a request id and keep context.self for streaming responses.
Message adapters must map the response into the asking actor's protocol, and a forgotten adapter silently drops the reply while the future still times out.
